reviews.author: ItsTheAnd
reviews.content:
Those who shun conspiracy theorists are displaying their own narcissism “I just want that person back (for me)”. Instead of projecting yourself onto them, the other approach is to engage your friend and actually look at the documented peer-reviewed evidence of the growing failures, corruption and deception of government, intelligence agencies and media. For any compassionate person these dark trends are vital to bring to awareness and enact change upon. 

Science spokespeople during covid gaslighted the public into feeling guilt and shame for making the rational point that we have immune systems that easily handle a flu like virus with a 99.9% survival rate, especially if treated with cheap, common and safe antivirals. Though there is no money in that therefore no incentive to affirm non-profitable scientific rigour. 

The government enforcement of an experimental vaccine that neither offered immunity nor safety fits the textbook definition of “abusive”. Lives have been destroyed not by a mild virus, but due to government overreach and the desperate ad-dollar funded media promoting a “safe and effective” treatment that was neither safe nor effective. Taxpayers will be paying off the covid debt decades into the future. “I was fine from my jab (therefore everyone else was too)” is pure narcissism and demonstrates low IQ all-or-nothing thinking. 

It’s well established that the CIA propagated the term ‘conspiracy theorist’ and that they purposefully promote hoax conspiracies to muddy the waters, distract from the true and evidenced conspiracies and discredit “the conspiracy movement” (there is no movement). All of these proofs are in their own archives open to the public. 

The solution to conspiracists is not to “save people” from realising truth according to your own standard of ignorance. It’s to boldly accept what the evidence is indicating, not live in wilful delusion. Vocalise your concern and solutions rationally, politely and hold yourself to a higher standard of intelligent inquiry. 

If you’d like to understand how the world really works consider listening to “coffee with Scott adams” podcast and join others who’ve become aware of our societal and institutional deceptions and how to navigate truthfully in this increasingly 1984ish reality.

reviews.author: Tate Causea
reviews.content:
Very disappointed in this episode. If I could give it zero I would. Biased is a word that applies here. 

To suggest that “conspiracy theorists” attract a certain type of individual with a certain type of ‘mentality’ is nonsense. It’s also insulting, especially to people who bother to listen, read and research contentious subject matter. 

For starters some conspiracies have turned out to be true, but lumping everyone together as conspiracy theorists is contempt prior to investigation. It’s prejudiced and judgemental. Having this attitude / approach is a much bigger problem than being a conspiracy theorist! It allows corruption to continue. 

Sure some conspiracies are just total garbage, but some definitely aren’t. Anyone with an ability to reason and think critically can understand this and tell the difference. 

It’s naive to think that scientific institutions, governments and every other set of power relations is going to be objective, transparent and honest. The reality is however that corruption exists everywhere, and it’s most commonly found in positions of power. “Power corrupts, and absolute power corrupts absolutely” as the quote goes.

reviews.author: Mollydoggles
reviews.content:
There was a lot of emphasis on how horrible having BPD is from the mental health sufferers side but little mentioned on how destructive and horrible it is to be at the very mercy of those with BPD. 
My workplace and my colleagues have suffered terribly from the utter ‘train wreck’ style that is working with a colleague with this diagnosis.From my experience there is very little understanding and empathy from those with BPD toward anyone else. And I DO NOT agree with that OT that the individual should conceal their diagnosis with management. 
How else can a workplace plan ahead for times of hostility and violent mood swings of the Staff member with BPD?
Sorry but that was a reckless comment.
Perhaps Sana, you could level the scales by having episodes that explore the experiences of those that live or work with someone with the multitude of mental health diagnoses you cover.
Couldn’t hurt seeing the issue from both sides.
See them as bookends.

reviews.author: zzzzz_1
reviews.content:
I really love this podcast. Sometimes it does brush over topics very broadly in a way that seemingly goes against its aims. 

The episode on attachment does the exact thing the podcast is criticising social media users of doing. Allowing a researcher to say that the concept of mental load appeared only a few years ago in public consciousness through a French cartoon in a blog is absurd. This absolutely ignores the long history of Feminist, black, queer and revolutionary work in this space. 

Bowlby was also not the first person to consider how the environment impacts a baby’s development - psychoanalysts had already been doing that for decades and Bowlby always acknowledged this. He was the first person to tie it to evolutionary biology.

Two very significant inconsistencies when you are claiming to set the record straight for all. 

Really love the podcast, but it is much more successful when it doesn’t have a snide tone.

reviews.author: Trexmonst
reviews.content: I get really concerned when “vanity” Is appealed to in order sell books. “High achievers” who chronically seek external validation and look at social media are in fact, garden variety insecure and anxious. It is INSUFFERABLE for a normal healthy actual high achiever ( without the vanity tag ) to be around people who whinge, compete look at social media like a teenager and seek praise. If your boss is a healthy person, your insecurity will reek ahead of you in any room you enter. And you will not become what your empty aspirations say you “should”. It’s pure vanity. Learn to self soothe. Learn to do a job without external gratification. Be quiet and get on with it without asking for prayer. Ughhh.

title: Background Briefing - ABC listen
description: The Background Briefing podcast brings you true stories not everyone will want you to hear, told by trusted reporters across Australia.

episodes.title: 01 In Search of the Missing Artist | The sculptor
episodes.description: The sales pitch goes that Jean Paul Mangin is a reclusive Parisian sculptor whose works are internationally acclaimed. His pieces sell quickly through one particular Australian gallery, sought after by trendy interior designers.

episodes.title: Introducing | In Search of the Missing Artist
episodes.description: For years, art buyers have been told that this man is an internationally acclaimed, intensely private Parisian sculptor. His bold, brightly coloured plastic works are available through one Melbourne gallery, and they're selling fast.

episodes.title: 03 The Road to Bondi | Deepfake
episodes.description: How did a wounded Bondi survivor become the face of a global deepfake conspiracy in less than 24 hours? Arsen Ostrovsky was celebrating Chanukah at Bondi Beach when the first shots rang out.

episodes.title: 02 The Road to Bondi | A Test of Character
episodes.description: This man fled Iran after being imprisoned and tortured for protesting the regime. Known only as AB, he came to Australia hoping to start again — and, in many ways, he did. He found love and started a family.

episodes.title: 01 The Road to Bondi | Father and Son
episodes.description: You think you know the story. You know how it ended. But you don’t know how it began. In the first episode of The Road to Bondi, reporter Josh Robertson traces the decades-long path that led a father and son to carry out their plan.

episodes.title: TRAILER — Introducing The Road to Bondi
episodes.description: In an ordinary Australian suburb, a father and son are secretly planning something terrible. One fateful summer evening, their path brings them crashing into the lives of strangers from around the world whose own stories haven’t yet been told.

episodes.title: 06 Hometown Boys | Not the only one
episodes.description: Insiders from the Harrow-Balmoral football club decide to break the code of silence. For Elise, it’s time to rebuild her life. But her story inspires other women to emerge with their own troubling accounts of the town’s club culture.

episodes.title: 05 Hometown Boys | 'Luke, Maybe'
episodes.description: A key witness submits a startling new statement that topples the guilty verdict and forces a retrial. This time, the men accused will not give evidence. But Lisa Hutchins, the trusted bush nurse will take the stand again — now for the defence.

episodes.title: 04 Hometown Boys | The Trial
episodes.description: As the criminal trial unfolds, witnesses from Balmoral waver on the stand, and the judge is "taken aback". The courtroom is heaving with supporters of the accused but the verdict is not what they're expecting.

episodes.title: 03 Hometown Boys | The 'Mayoress of Balmoral'
episodes.description: A respected bush nurse with close ties to the accused becomes a key police witness. As the investigation quietly gathers pace, locals start to choose sides and the family of the victim feels ostracised.

reviews.author: NTAussie
reviews.content:
I listened to Background Briefing’s episode Hometown Boys with a heavy heart.

What happened to Elise was serious, devastating harm. Her experience, and the failures that allowed it to occur, deserve to be named clearly and held with honesty and accountability. My deepest sympathy is with Elise and her family, whose pain and loss should never be minimised or explained away.

I grew up in Balmoral, and my family has deep roots there also. It is a close-knit and caring community, even as it faces real and complex challenges today. That sense of connection and responsibility shaped me, I became a social worker because of that town.

I have two siblings with disability who were known, included, and valued growing up. People looked out for them. That experience also matters, and it too is part of Balmoral’s story.

While this episode powerfully highlighted harm and accountability, it felt like it reflected only a narrow subset of the community. Other voices and acts of care were largely absent, leaving the picture incomplete.

I hope future storytelling can hold more than one truth at once: the reality of profound harm, and the reality of communities that must reckon with it while still being capable of care, inclusion, and change

reviews.author: Sahpee
reviews.content:
It doesn’t matter if it’s a village in India, or a town in Victoria. After an horrific rape, the community prioritises the hierarchy and protecting the perpetrators. The community perpetuates the disgusting, criminal behaviour by gaslighting and bullying the victim instead of holding the perpetrators to account.
The victim and family pay over and over again throughout the fight for justice. These footy clubs are cesspools that perpetuate racism, violence, drink/drug culture, bullying and sexual violence, all carefully hidden under the thin veneer of sporting achievement. What hope do young boys have coming into this environment, especially if they live in the middle of nowhere and this club is the one option for social connection?

reviews.author: JacL25
reviews.content: Hometown Boys was a wonderful series. I hope it stops some people in their tracks to consider their response. This shows just how much a football club can influence the culture of a town. For the worse instead of better. Very few people showed courage and integrity in this ‘Elyce’ and her family showed  immense integrity and are the only ones who deserve to hold their head high. As a nurse I am disgusted in Lisa, advocating for the vulnerable is at the core of being a nurse……. You were misaligned with who were the vulnerable people here and i hope that the guilt you must feel is heavy to hold. This has shone a spotlight not only on Balmoral but on all small towns to consider what culture they have and what they stand for.

reviews.author: Samantha105
reviews.content: We live in a country where men are killing their partners frequently. I actually love Background briefing as a podcast, but wow this episode 2 of road to Bondi is almost mind boggling. Making excuses for a man who is in jail for assaulting (again) his pregnant partner because he ‘made some bad choices’ who is now going to be deported as he isn’t a citizen and continually ends up in jail, but oh - hang on we should treat him differently, because he was in the wrong place, at the wrong time - but did a good thing? I think this is what is exactly wrong with our legal system, and why people like him get chance, after chance, moving closer to the line before they cross over it. And someone dies….

reviews.author: Steph J C
reviews.content: Such a great podcast. Thank you to Elise for standing up and doing what a lot of women feel they can’t. It would have been incredibly tough to keep going and go to Court twice. You would no doubt have helped a lot of others in your situation for speaking out. Home Town Boys was really moving. She is incredibly strong and I just couldn’t believe her friends didn’t get up and get around her. What a traumatic experience she went through and to not have the support would have been so difficult. Also the courage of the few in the community that did speak out in support, hopefully more will stand up after listening to this.

reviews.author: Hoodooguru81
reviews.content:
Roy & HG mean the world to me.
They instantly transport me back to my childhood in the 80’s and 90’s where I would listen to them on Triple J whilst playing pool in my fathers shed as a young boy growing up in South West Sydney. 
Stepping into their world for an hour each week is something I hold dear, especially in this time when most are locked up in their homes. 
How does one sum up Roy and HG quickly? 
Think of stepping into the rabbit hole in Alice In Wonderland and entering into a magical world where too much sport is barely enough. A part truth, part fictional world that will leave you wondering have I entered the fifth dimension? 
Actually it’s more likened to tripping over a 6 foot divot left from a school fete tent in Watsford Oval, Lithgow. But you get the angle. 

Keep going as long as you can keep going guys. It is making a difference to many. 
Bless you both and Thankyou!

reviews.author: JonesBoy
reviews.content: There are very few social commentators who capture the essence of the “Australian Monday Morning Sporting Experts” quite as insightfully as these two chaps. For those who are new chums in our great country, may I politely suggest that listening to their programs will not really help you understand what it is to be an Aussie but the experience sure will introduce you to that clever knack that so many real Orstraylyuns have of kicking down the doors of boorish respectability and fake humility without being rude! Long may they rule over the tracks, fields, pools, gymnasiums and change rooms of our young but great nation.

reviews.author: Ba5tien
reviews.content: Gentlemen I’ve followed your antics for years as I ‘bludged’ on my way to training for (and winning) Aussie Gold in aerobics, through marathon training, travelling home from underwater hockey training, hours of surf boat training and learning rugby. I _love_ that these days women get at least an occasional mention. In the beginning I found myself shouting at the radio a bit as you lamented poor performances by Aussie men, but women weren’t mentioned. Glad times are changing

reviews.author: Women like great films too!
reviews.content: Maybe it’s because I am not Australian by birth… but this is one of the unfunniest things I have ever heard.  It’s just inane gibbering to me.  They seem to be cracking each other up - but certainly not me!  The talk about cat meat in France is also slightly xenophobic considering they don’t eat cat meat in France?? They say they will eat anything on France but hello - crocodile and kangaroo? Just not funny to me, sorry.

reviews.author: CarolineGinger
reviews.content:
I find myself in different Oz cities for work, so I’ve been listening to this podcast on my walks while getting some exercise…I’ve been laughing so hard that I have to stop, and I’m sure I look like a total nutcase laughing to myself 🤣 

Note - those that don’t know these guys, please watch The Dream/The Ice Dream

Love you Roy and HG, never change!

title: Conversations with Richard Fidler and Sarah Kanowski - ABC listen
description: Conversations draws you deeper into the life story of someone you may, or may not, have heard about — someone who has seen and done amazing things.

episodes.title: The story behind Sydney’s Luna Park and its impact on the city
episodes.description: Author Helen Pitt has written a history of the iconic fun park and it's a tale bound up with con men, crooked cops, and developers who have long wanted to snatch up the prime piece of waterfront real estate.

episodes.title: Encore: What I learnt about Australia as an Outback GP
episodes.description: When Sonia Henry signed up to work as a GP in a remote mining town in the Pilbara, the experience changed almost everything she believed about Australia.

episodes.title: Why my father was abandoned and the empathy I now have for his mother
episodes.description: Jane Messer grew up with a loving father who never really understood why as a child his mother left him and his older sister at a boarding school, so she decided to find out the full story and prove that he was in fact, loved.

episodes.title: Encore: The hidden corners of Emma's Hong Kong — fishing villages, beaches and ancestral graveyards
episodes.description: Novelist Emma Pei Yin ran away from Hong Kong as a teenager to start fresh in Australia. But she found herself repeatedly drawn back home whenever she put pen to paper.

episodes.title: 'The century of foundlings'—what Cynthia found when she went looking maternal family secrets
episodes.description: Writer Cynthia Banham on discovering the shocking truth about her great-grandmother, reckoning with buried family secrets, and the criticisms mothers face from others and sometimes most harshly, from themselves.

episodes.title: Spotting the psychopaths, sadists and narcissists in our lives and how to get rid of them
episodes.description: Toxic people are around us in our workplaces, our families and our dating lives. Research psychologist Leanne ten Brinke is here to tell you how to spot them, and get rid of them from your orbit.

episodes.title: Encore: How his ex-wife's hidden letter changed everything for Teddy Tahu Rhodes
episodes.description: Born with a magnificent voice, Opera star Teddy Tahu Rhodes fought against his destiny for years until a letter he'd been avoiding reading changed everything (R)

episodes.title: The GP clinic for patients often overlooked by society
episodes.description: Dr Nada Andric wants to improve the health of people who are marginalised in the community and their access to healthcare.

episodes.title: Encore: Bo Seo on good arguments and the power of disagreement
episodes.description: Two-time World Debating champion Bo Seo on how love and listening can improve how we disagree, so we're not at each other's throats online and offline (R). When Bo was 8 years old, he and his parents migrated from Korea to Australia.

episodes.title: Exploring loss, love and meaning with psychoanalyst Stephen Grosz
episodes.description: Stephen Grosz has welcomed people into his office for more than 40 years, and believes our greatest task in life is to see ourselves and others with more clarity, in order to live more easily and with more please.

reviews.author: Hermy7
reviews.content: I have listened to Conversations for years and although it has gotten progressively more woke over the last few years, I have mostly still enjoyed it, especially the hosts. Richard and Sarah are great. This episode from the Brisbane writers festival was the widest I’ve ever heard. The guest is so incredibly deranged when it comes to Trump that he obviously can’t even bring himself to fact check his claims and assertions about the President. He made so many false claims that I can’t even begin to list them. He clearly lives in the bubble of NYC journalists & TV celebrities that have no idea about the lives of their fellow Americans. The “holier than thou” was dripping everywhere and unfortunately Richard was lapping it up along with the smug laughs and claps from the audience. Why we have to pay over a billion dollars a year for this kind of production is beyond me.

reviews.author: Mollydoggles
reviews.content:
I have been listening to Conversations for over 12 years and it’s been very enlightening at times.
But interviewing an ex-MAFS contestant???
I’d rather hear( and more likely believe) a story about an individual who believes they had a close encounter with an alien rather than this claptrap from a ‘holistic’ counsellor who doesn’t watch TV but uses ‘conscious’ communication!Insert rolling of eyes here. 

If I heard Lucinda Light say one more time about ‘digging deep’ I was probably going to dig my own hole and bury myself to stop it.
You’ve had some wonderful guests and stories on over the past but please leave the woeful ‘wokeness actors’ for other podcasts.
It was EXCRUCIATING and below your standards.

reviews.author: Blue From Tassie
reviews.content: I used to love this show when it was just Richard Fiedler. Now we have the sycophantic Sarah Kinofsky and even worse, the vapid Sana Qadar. Listening to Sana Qadar giggle her way through the episode on psychopathy with Jon Robson while providing nothing of substance to the conversation  with the guest was nauseating. Yet another once great ABC show that has become a dumpster fire of the banal. Honestly, the ABC used to be synonymous with quality broadcasting but these days it leaves me wondering why we are wasting tax payer money on this.

reviews.author: Beth in Canberra
reviews.content:
The quality of the conversations hasn’t diminished in all the years I’ve tuned in💜.
The variety of guest, the emotion each person brings, the content you didn’t even know you would be interested in!
I love Sarah’s laugh when she’s genuinely amused and Richard’s sense of humour hits the mark every time.
I’m travelling in Chile & Argentina at present & am busily downloading some convos to help me get across the Drakes Passage en route to see a penguin or two! Thx for all the research & work to pull Conversations together.

reviews.author: Vonn5
reviews.content: I seem to spend most of my time on my own so having a ‘conversation’ to listen to is a staple part of that. When I think back on long drives to visit family or the occasional adventure, or projects I’ve finished, there’s usually a conversation or two associated with each of these. It help me to stay humble listening to the hardships some have had to endure, and appreciate some opportunities I’ve had that others didn’t. And sometimes they’re just entertaining. Thank you for ‘Conversations’.

title: Expanse with Dominique Bayens - ABC listen
description: In 1999 a young American dumped his bicycle and walked out into the Great Sandy Desert in remote northern Australia. He was an Alaskan firefighter, seemingly with everything to live for. So why did he risk it all to go into the wilderness alone? And how do you search for someone who doesn't want to be found? New episodes released each Wednesday

episodes.title: BONUS | Who was Tony Popic?
episodes.description: Since the podcast started rolling out, a lot of people have got in touch with information. Two people have been able to shed light on some previously unknown parts of the story.

episodes.title: 06 Expanse: The Nannup Four | Northcliffe
episodes.description: A family friend and former policeman continues to search for answers for Jim and Cath McDougall decades after the Nannup four vanished. The family and friends of Chantelle McDougall try to find their own answers, as one last glimmer of hope emerges.

episodes.title: 05 Expanse: The Nannup Four | Simon says
episodes.description: Jim and Cath McDougall are left reeling as the true depth of Simon Kadwill’s deception is revealed.

episodes.title: 04 Expanse: The Nannup Four | A question of belief
episodes.description: Tony Popic is talking about an end of days, Simon is seeing spirits and Chantelle is forced into a difficult decision as increasingly troubling hints something's not right come to light.

episodes.title: 03 Expanse: The Nannup Four | Down the rabbit hole
episodes.description: Dominique travels across the country to meet the two people who might be able to help her understand how Chantelle came to be living a reclusive life in a hidden corner of Western Australia, alongside a self-styled spiritual guru 18 years her senior.

episodes.title: 02 Expanse: The Nannup Four | Selling snake oil
episodes.description: A chance encounter in the streets of Melbourne in 1998 leaves a friend wondering what Chantelle McDougall has been pulled into. Dominique hears about the escalating pattern of control Simon Kadwill exercises over Chantelle.

episodes.title: 01 Expanse: The Nannup Four | The people in the blue house
episodes.description: When three adults and a child disappear without a trace from the isolated bush community of Nannup in 2007, it sparks disturbing theories about what might have happened.

episodes.title: Expanse: The Nannup Four
episodes.description: When four people disappeared from a blue farmhouse on the outskirts of the Western Australian town of Nannup in 2007, they left behind the scatterings of a life, a note pinned to their door and a question: was the disappearance a choice... or murder?

episodes.title: BONUS Expanse: Nowhere Man | Gunslinger
episodes.description: The search for Robert Bogucki brought together a cast of colourful characters, including a cigar-toting, moustachioed American named Garrison ‘Gunslinger’ St Clair.

episodes.title: 06 Expanse: Nowhere Man | Lost and found
episodes.description: A quarter of a century after he survived the Great Sandy Desert, Robert Bogucki is back for an odd-couple road trip with the Aboriginal tracker who helped search for him all those years ago.

reviews.author: Vida Sydney
reviews.content:
In Japan, especially in large cities, parts of the sex industry are controlled by the Japanese mafia (yakuza). This is not mentioned in the interview. Instead, the journalist generalises the behaviour of the entire population.

In Japan, it is not normal to have affairs, as she suggests. Saying that it is normal for husbands to have affairs is completely incorrect. Many wives sue their husbands for infidelity, which can result in significant financial penalties and negatively affect the husband’s parental rights.

It is also important to state that many snack bar jobs are run by yakuza groups. Once someone starts working in these places, they are likely to come into contact with people connected to these gangs, which can be very dangerous.

The Clare Campbell also mentions that the victim had a sister who worked in other places and that nothing happened to her. This should not be used to give false hope to young girls.

Japan is safer than many other countries, but that does not mean you cannot one day encounter a psychopath. Sick people exist everywhere.
There is no such thing as easy money. If something seems too good to be true, you should run.

reviews.author: Trexmonst
reviews.content: This case is interesting in that it is replicated in a less “sensational” manner in all domestic violence situations. The misrepresentation of intimacy when seeking a coercive control deception and power over situations.  The manipulative and exploitative nature of people who want to extort care and affection from a spouse. Male violence against women has so many facets of this type of deception and exploitation and - it’s usually where no one else can see, behind closed doors. This case is SO disgusting and Caitlin is entirely untrustworthy. She will do if shah. Any way she can. She isn’t remorseful, she is faking remorse.

reviews.author: bia-h
reviews.content:
I first listened because my daughter was interviewed about her podcast  ‘The Nurse’ after it was released.
I find each episode to be a refreshing change from the ‘ reporting’ style of most true crime podcasts. The guests are eloquent and extremely varied personalities and no two episodes are the same. Definitely a great listen!

reviews.author: vinnieaudrey

title: Global Roaming with Geraldine Doogue and Hamish Macdonald and Kylie Morris and Latika Bourke - ABC listen
description: Award-winning journalists Geraldine Doogue and Hamish Macdonald are joined by two new hosts, former foreign correspondent Kylie Morris and journalist Latika Bourke in London. Every day, they'll be discussing the biggest world events and how to make of sense of them.

episodes.title: Keir Starmer is ‘fed up’ and so are the British. Is the UK doomed?
episodes.description: Brexit, the COVID-19 pandemic, shifting global headwinds and now the war in the Middle East have hit the British hard. So with some of the world's highest energy costs and a stretched defence force, what does the future hold?

episodes.title: How Hungary trumped Orbán
episodes.description: Péter Magyar has beaten Viktor Orbán in Hungary's election, ending 16 years of autocratic rule. Hundreds of thousands of Hungarians celebrated in the streets of Budapest as the results were announced.

episodes.title: Peacemaker or playmaker? Where China stands on Trump's war in the Middle East
episodes.description: The war in the Middle East is sending shock waves through global supply chains, so where does this leave economic superpower China? Will it emerge as a genuine global leader or merely make a profit from global disorder?

episodes.title: Is Israel using Lebanon to sabotage peace in the Middle East?
episodes.description: The ink hadn't even dried on the initial US-Iran ceasefire last week when Israel launched an unprecedented bombardment on Lebanon's capital, Beirut.

episodes.title: A Matter of Facts: Wikipedia co-founder on freedom of speech vs disinformation
episodes.description: Is Wikipedia a relic of a more utopian version of the internet? Or is it the citizen-led antidote that we need?

episodes.title: Could Australia and Asia supply our own energy and cut out the Middle East?
episodes.description: The Middle East conflict has triggered a reckoning in global energy supplies.

episodes.title: Can Cubans survive under Trump's fist?
episodes.description: The war in Iran has aroused worldwide fears: what happens if a country runs out of oil? Because of severe US restrictions, Cuba has faced that reality, having been without oil for three months.

episodes.title: Trump and the Iran ceasefire: what happens next?
episodes.description: A ceasefire is declared after Donald Trump agrees to a two-week pause in attacks on Iran, contingent on the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. But is this a genuine de-escalation or a strategic pause?

episodes.title: Soft power, hard lesson: what can Australia learn from unhappy Asian students?
episodes.description: Australia's education system is one of our most successful export industries, worth an estimated 54 billion dollars.

episodes.title: A Matter of Facts: How mainstream media lost public trust
episodes.description: In our previous Matter of Facts mini-series episodes, we covered why our brains are vulnerable to misinformation, and how disinformation is affecting democracies. Today, we examine the public's trust (or lack thereof) in mainstream media.

reviews.author: Water bus
reviews.content:
I respect Geraldine and Hamish as journalists but I don’t really want to hear their opinions and interpretations on world affairs for 5 minutes at the start and end of the podcast. Maybe Geraldine and Hamish would argue they’re “contextualising” the topic at hand but I tend to think they just use the time to give their own opinions and interpretation of the topic.
Cutting the opinion segments would enable a longer interview with the guests - and currently the interviews are too short especially given there’s two hosts trying to ask questions. 

The choice of guests also tends to be lacking in originality and generally only offers a Western centric pro-US view of the world, mainly interviewing people from the the foreign policy establishment (eg Chatham House, anti-Trump commentators etc). I wouldn’t mind this if the guests got asked critical questions challenging their arguments and logic, but unfortunately Geraldine and Hamish’s questions tend to be very vague, which means we don’t get much of a stimulating debate. Also you can just turn on the tv and radio and hear the same kinds of establishment views so what is Global Roaming offering that’s new or different?

Interviewing Kishore Mahbubani and Hugh White is a good start as they think a bit differently to the Western establishment, but again the interviews were pretty short and tended to have unfocused, long-winded questions like asking Mahbubani about whether democracy has innate strengths, and I’m just not sure why that was relevant to the bigger picture of the Asian century and the changing international environment.

It’s good that the abc still has a podcast like this dedicated to international politics but I think the podcast could make a fair few improvements.

reviews.author: Dean M99
reviews.content: The GR team’s recent summer series on the Aukus debacle is a rare exception in the Australian media landscape of in-depth analysis of the pure folly of the Aukus announcement, and the disastrous impact it has had on Australia’s relationships with its immediate neighbours and its biggest trading partner China. The Aukus ‘deal’, which was foisted on the long-suffering Australian public by former Prime Minister Morrison in a media stunt with outgoing US President Joe Biden and former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson in 2022, and then adopted in unseemly haste (following a 2 hour consideration by shadow Cabinet) by the then Labor Opposition, has not faced any serious scrutiny in the largely pro-Washington mainstream media in Australia, but there have been some low-level questions asked (for example by Australian Greens Senator David Shoebridge during Senate Estimates), and some excellent books and journal articles investigating the shadowy figures who brought the ‘deal’ to fruition, and some, like former Prime Ministers Turnbull and Keating, querying the wisdom of the  whole thing. ‘deal’

reviews.author: Primary_Persephone
reviews.content:
I really value the perspective that Geraldine brings to the podcast. One of the reasons I am a regular listener of the pod is because it isn’t an echo chamber - the conversations challenge assumptions and encourage people to think more deeply about complex global issues.

Her comment about the Iranian people needing to find a way to rise up / find a solution has attracted criticism - and quite a strong response from Hamish- but I think it was pointing to a broader historial reality: meaningful and sustainable political change often has to come from within societies themselves. Acknowledging that doesn’t ignore the enormous risks that people face under authoritarian regimes nor does it dismiss the incredible courage shown by many Iranians. 

Thanks Geraldine and Hamish for creating the space for this types of conversations - especially in a time where people have lost the ability to disagree constructively. It’s appreciated.

title: Health Report with Norman Swan and Dr Preeya Alexander - ABC listen
description: Covering the health stories that make a difference. Dr Norman Swan and Dr Preeya Alexander dissect the latest and breaking news in the medical world.

episodes.title: Treating a medical emergency ... in space
episodes.description: When a medical emergency happens in space, how is it treated? And what does life in Antarctica have to teach us about staying healthy on a spaceflight?

episodes.title: What to expect this flu season
episodes.description: Which flu strains are likely to be dominant this flu season - and what's the story with the new nasal spray vaccine? Speaking of sprays ... there's a simple saline spray that might help kids with sleep apnoea avoid surgery.

episodes.title: 3D printing in healthcare
episodes.description: 3D printing is becoming an incredibly versatile modern tool - with scope to apply it to engineering, manufacturing, architecture and design challenges. And it's increasingly being used in ... healthcare.

episodes.title: Ultra-processed foods and behaviour in kids
episodes.description: There's been major buzz in recent years over ultra-processed foods and whether they may be harmful to our health.

episodes.title: MDMA therapy's side effects
episodes.description: MDMA psychotherapy was approved in Australia three years ago. Who's using it and what do we know about treatment side effects? Vaccine reminders can help nudge people back on track, but how the message is framed matters.

episodes.title: Are Australian kids eating too much salt?
episodes.description: Are Australian schoolkids eating too much salt? And does it put them at risk of high blood pressure? A new approach to breast cancer screening based on risk could reduce the number of screens needed for some women.

episodes.title: Can AI chatbots be good therapists?
episodes.description: We know many people are turning to generative AI for health advice, including tips on how to manage stress, anxiety and low mood.

episodes.title: Wait, does exercise help osteoarthritis?
episodes.description: A paper has suggested exercise has minimal, short-term effects on osteoarthritis. But experts are warning people with the condition that they shouldn't stop moving.

episodes.title: Prescribing exercise for mental health
episodes.description: Researchers have pin-pointed the best exercise routines for depression or anxiety symptoms, and they might be equal to medication and talk therapy. Also, why states and territories are making changes to their maternity care guidance for doctors.

episodes.title: The cost shock of specialist care
episodes.description: When you pay for private health insurance, you might assume you'll be well covered if you get injured or fall ill. But a new report has revealed the huge costs that catch people off guard, and sometimes prevent them from receiving care.

reviews.author: Paikea Ngati Porou
reviews.content:
Just listened to the gender bias in medical research and treatment. So appalling to hear men have been the guinea pigs in medical trials. I’m glad that women will now will also be guinea pigs. 

It reminds me of shocking Tuskegee Syphillis trial where black men’s syphilis was left untreated for decades - treating them as a control group. Being guinea pigs for medical research has been and continues to be risky for the participant, even if in the long march of medicine it is beneficial.

One overall measure of bias of the healthcare between men and women is that life expectancy of men is about 3 years less than women in Australia .  Let’s keep  an eye on that disparity - it is not biologically destiny -  it is a product of society & culture. Focus on what is causing men to die quicker than men - a century ago this was not the case. Don’t just trig the tired stuff about men ( abd  in a similar light indigenous ) are responsible for their shorter lives.

If the opposite was happening we would hear a completely different spinning  - ie only women were medical guinea pigs and if women lived 3 years less than men on average there would be an uproar. Why no uproar when it happened to men.

A larger bias in medical research and medical treatment is the non-indigenous  population & the indigenous population. The Pacific peoples were isolated & have specific needs - a biological, but under appreciated,  fact. We die neatly 10-15 years younger!

I am tired of the ABC’s  misandrist and racial  bias. Please add dispassionate, even-handed scientific light, rather than ideological  bias

reviews.author: Inky's self knowledge
reviews.content:
I listened to the Health Report story broadcast re above subject, particularly regarding the second part that mentioned brain images - default mode network and my comments are generally to do with ‘closing down the ego’s memory hub’. 
The question arising out of the broadcast is whether this function of the brain/mind is able to be silenced naturally without recourse to taking psychedelic substances or indeed hypo ventilation by inducing specific breathing practices. 
So is there another possibility of altering the default mode network by self knowledge that doesn’t involve mentally induced effort to provide energy that is necessary for a change in the regulatory hub functioning. And what might happen in the event that the ego is nullified?
Jiddu Krishnamurti espoused that something akin to this closing down the walls of ego is demanded in moving from a fragmented structure of consciousness to an holistic state of consciousness and this aspect of Krishnamurti’s teachings has intrigued me to learn about its effects on daily living. I am open to communicating with others regarding this matter.

reviews.author: Newcastle OZ.
reviews.content: There was a movement some years ago for patients to be referred to as clients.  I found this alarming, now there is a bid to claim that being a person   should outranks the unique status of being a patient. I believe that health professionals should always be mindful of the depth of meaning embedded in that word patient. As a client an individual would have no expectation of the invasive /intrusive nature of the relationship with a health professional. As has been described- intimate strangers. I am health literate but I am seeking expertise and, yes, explanation from ‘my’ health professional. Meanwhile, I want that individual to treat me as a patient. Reclaiming the word - patient-with all the depth implied for a respectful interaction. Beyond the superficiality of either being a client or a person. Words are nuanced please don’t  denude our language. Reclaim

title: If You're Listening with Matt Bevan - ABC listen

title: Late Night Live with David Marr - ABC listen
description: Incisive analysis, fearless debates and nightly surprises. Explore the serious, the strange and the profound with David Marr.

episodes.title: A Jewish Australian lawyer reckons with state violence. Plus, can corporate scandals be good for the world?

title: No One Saw It Coming with Marc Fennell - ABC listen
description: The bit players, the unexpected twists, the turning point you missed. Join Walkley award-winner Marc Fennell as he uncovers the incredible moments that changed the course of history.

episodes.title: Ancient Greek built a steam engine for dinner parties
episodes.description: Long before steam trains, before factories, before the Industrial Revolution, someone figured out how to turn steam into motion.

episodes.title: She gave her son smallpox. Her bet paid off.
episodes.description: It was one of the deadliest diseases known to humankind. And just 50 years ago it was officially eradicated. But there’s someone missing from the story of smallpox.

episodes.title: Cocaine wine: The Pope’s energy drink
episodes.description: If you looked at it, you wouldn’t bat an eyelid, but this red wine had something in it that today could land you in jail. It was drunk and endorsed by presidents, royalty and even popes and made its maker a millionaire.

episodes.title: A horse race and a murderer invented cinema

episodes.title: Starving for freedom: The prison death that changed Ireland

episodes.title: Let slaves dance: The secret of New Orleans jazz

episodes.title: She faked insanity. Then became a star.

episodes.title: The mafia bar riot that sparked gay pride
episodes.description: 28 June 1969 was a regular Saturday night at the Stonewall Inn. Until it wasn’t.

episodes.title: The royal roots of French fries
episodes.description: ‘Would you like fries with that?’ It’s a question you’ve likely been asked countless times. But what if the only reason French fries are so popular throughout the West today is because of a Queen who lost her head during the French Revolution?

episodes.title: Three words brought down the Berlin Wall

But this is a great example I think, for people to perhaps try to gain something from - that’s actually gonna be helpful for them, instead of being more harmful for them & maybe they can try to learn what they’re listening to is actually not the truth directly, but rather a lesson in brain training to improve their skills in how to be able to easily distinguish between the so called truth & seperate that from the facts, or should I say, the stupid mainstream story- ie. the history that we’re all been told our whole lives & look past it to start seeing how this manipulation that the media have done to us - is not a conspiracy theory - but the reality that is difficult for everyone to grasp, it’s not too hard to start picking up on what is happening & you’ll hear the truth resonate in a different way than the bulls**t  & the sooner we can all start doing that - the better we will all be! reviews.author: Rara I

reviews.author: Michael_in_Au

Not too long, always a fascinating topic presented by Marc and an expert on the topic in a clear, scientific, style that has just enough banter to make you smile while not distracting from the topic.

reviews.author: nickinbronte

title: Not Stupid with Julia Baird and Jeremy Fernandez - ABC listen
description: Julia Baird and Jeremy Fernandez chat about the stories you're obsessed with, the stuff you've missed and the things that matter.

reviews.author: RobnJPerthAus
reviews.content:
I'll start with what would usually be an entire review, or the last line of a review: definitely worth a listen.

Stories of people embroiled in scientific endeavours; Stories from people's lives, understood through science; & Science's uncertainties (or are they?) presented for us to think on and maybe, act on.

The maker of this program (the host, who seems to be at the helm of this program) has combined her scientific credentials with her years in radio gathering & telling stories. This podcast feels like the culmination of all she's done so far, with the result being really interesting stories that come out of science.

From the enthralling first episode of amazing storytelling about some *epic* science, to the final episode of the first season about some very close-to-home science that will send many to the Science Friction website looking for more information, this podcast is the stuff of legends and the stories around the evidence of science.

The episodes are a good length, starting with a couple around 35 minutes to accomodate the dramatic & profound stories they tell. Then it's down to shorter episodes, packed with enough science to give you the guts of it in digestible terms, surrounded by the stories that relate the science firmly to the experiences of people.

Sometimes a story is of a scientific field that's relatively new but widely accepted, or as in the final episode, science that has been debated for years. And not just debated because science is progressed by further findings that support (or don't), expand, or contest what has come before. We hear the differing views of scientists working on research into the same issue - and that's excluding the interest groups that have an agenda for one outcome to be "the right outcome". But they're represented too: in the last episode of season one, an industry group who chose not to be interviewed provide their statement for us to read.

I usually wanted to get more of an understanding on topics covered, sometimes out of interest, and sometimes because I had a decision to make: was there evidence that would lead me to change my behaviour or decisions? Episode 6, as I mentioned, is an example of that & will have many heading to the website with their questions. And there are different answers for everyone depending on their circumstances and their response to what's presented.

And, as the host says, there's the rub.

@RobnWithAWhy

reviews.author: So cello
reviews.content:
Frustrating interview on the part of the journalist who seemed hellbent on extracting a biased commentary from the otherwise measured, interesting interviewee scientists. The interviewer interjected with comments which contradicted the scientists being interviewed? Why? 

This is sad because the subject was fascinating. 

Next time please focus on the story of the science and allow the interviewers to provide the facts of the matter. 

What makes matters worse, there were rather offensive things implied in respect of Chinese scientists in general: that they are more likely to act “rogue”, quite rightly the interviewer was put in her place by the two western scientists being interviewed  who made parallels to the experience with IVF innovators who also went “rogue”. 

ABC: check your bias.

reviews.author: Peter Cats
reviews.content: While the topics were entertaining and the show has a high production value. Many of the points being made were not convincing and too soft on evidence, generally asking the audience to just ‘go with it’ rather than the typical “facts first” approach from other ABC science podcasts/All in the mind/etc. Counterpoints weren’t explored further weakening the topics, and some of the interviewees were simply without credibility: spinning such absurdities as “one billion people having regular relationships with chatbots”, and glossing over a woman’s somewhat concerning motivation for valuing a romantic partner that doesn’t speak unless first spoken to.

Otherwise it's a great program.

title: ABC AFL DAILY with Corbin Middlemas and Ben Cameron - ABC listen
description: Corbin Middlemas and Ben Cameron are joined by a rotating cast of AFL legends, including some of the sharpest minds in the game, to pull apart the biggest stories in Aussie Rules.

episodes.title: Blues’ recurring nightmare as Nick Daicos storms his 100th game
episodes.description: Carlton once again squandered their lead, as Nick Daicos showed everyone why it’s worth celebrating his 100th game. Has the AFL had a more versatile player than Mark Blicavs? Does the Sydney derby deserve to be a standalone event?

episodes.title: The incentive of accusers and why Luke Beveridge is ruck-ist

episodes.title: AFL Monday: Chamberlain on Butters "nothing worse" you can say to an umpire

episodes.title: What did Zak Butters say and how do you improve Gather Round?

episodes.title: AFL Saturday: Ramanauskas on Wildcard Round - 'If you're going down the cash path, people are going to start laughing at you'

episodes.title: Gather Round is underway and can you put a price on hosting Wildcard Round?

episodes.title: Pickett power and are the Tigers getting away with how bad they’ve been?

episodes.title: AFL Saturday: Malthouse - 'This board has to be so strong to withstand what comes from outside'

title: ABC Business Daily with Carrington Clarke and Alan Kohler - ABC listen
description: The podcast that helps you unpack the latest business and finance news. Analysing the stories moving share markets, shaping industries and affecting the Australian economy. Monday to Thursday, ABC Senior Business Correspondent, Carrington Clarke, examines the biggest business news with ABC's specialist reporters. From finance to AI technology and politics, the team will break down what happened, why it matters and what it might mean for you and your financial future. On Fridays, trusted Australian financial journalist Alan Kohler hosts an in-depth interview with the decisions-makers, innovators and strategists who are shaping the economy. 'That’s Business with Alan Kohler', invites well-known CEOs, entrepreneurs and politicians in for a deep dive into the tough lessons learned and unspoken rules driving Australian business. Host Carrington Clarke is a former economist, ABC North America correspondent from Washington DC and East Asia correspondent from Seoul, He previously worked as a Sky News Journalist and Fairfax Media editor. He has also reported for ABC Investigations’ flagship current affairs television program ‘7.30’ and ‘The Business.’ Host Alan Kohler AM is a former editor of The Age, The Australian Financial Review (AFR) and a columnist for The Sydney Morning Herald and Chanticleer in AFR. He was also the business editor for ABC Investigations’ flagship current affairs television program ‘7.30’ and the host of ‘Inside Business.’ For more sharp insights, clear explanations, and business news coverage you can trust, hit follow or favourite to add new episodes of ABC Business Daily and That's Business with Alan Kohler to your playlist, on ABC listen app, or wherever you get your podcasts.

episodes.title: Fuelcast: What does the Viva fire mean for petrol?
episodes.description: The Prime Minister visited the Viva Energy refinery this morning, announcing that it is still operating, but at reduced capacity. What should Australians expect in terms of fuel supply against the backdrop of the ongoing energy crisis?

episodes.title: Australia has two refineries. One's been on fire
episodes.description: It was a shocking scene for most Australians to wake up to - the Viva Energy refinery ablaze. The fire has raised further questions about Australia’s vulnerability to cuts in fuel supply. Could biofuels be part of the answer?

episodes.title: A warning from the IMF
episodes.description: The world’s financial and economic elite are descending on Washington DC. The International Monetary Fund is holding a series of meetings and warning that the energy crisis is going to mean (at the very least) lower growth and higher inflation.

episodes.title: Fuelcast: Airlines feel the pain
episodes.description: Qantas says its fuel bill could be $600 million to $800 million higher than expected because of the ongoing energy crisis - and it plans to reduce capacity to help offset some of those costs.

episodes.title: Why can't Australia 'drill baby drill'?
episodes.description: This time, the US stuck to its deadline. Its navy is now blockading Iran’s ports, further limiting the flow of energy from the crucial Gulf region.

episodes.title: The 'retail politics' of fuel
episodes.description: After direct talks between the US and Iran concluded with no agreement, Donald Trump has raised the stakes by ordering a blockade of ships that visit Iranian ports. The move has stymied global energy flow and caused oil prices to jump. Again.

episodes.title: Bonus: ABC Business Daily's Fuelcast
episodes.description: Donald Trump has announced a US naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, while Anthony Albanese prepares to travel to Malaysia and Brunei after his recent trip to Singapore, as Australia looks to shore up its fuel security.

episodes.title: Can Paul Schroder save the Australian dream?
episodes.description: More than $400 billion. Millions of members. And a front-row seat to the forces shaping the Australian economy. If you think super is dull, or the people who run it are dull, think again.

episodes.title: The market reacts to a fragile ceasefire
episodes.description: Around the globe investors cheered the ceasefire agreement between the US and Iran, with surging stocks and an oil price plunge.

episodes.title: Trump TACOs and Australia buys EVs
episodes.description: It appeared the market was betting on another TACO Tuesday from Donald Trump. And it could be said that he’s delivered.

reviews.author: Aaaaaaaaaaaaahnne
reviews.content: This podcast used to deliver cutting political analysis, but sadly seems to have gone  downhill in the last couple of years. The seeming inability to objectively report facts on an unfolding genocide and challenge the political establishment on its inaction and hypocrisy has been surprising and disappointing. Whether this is a reflection of broader censorship and culture problems at the ABC recently exposed in Antoinette Lattouf’s legal case, or of personal biases of the hosts remains unclear. Regardless I cannot stomach to listen anymore.

reviews.author: Tig42
reviews.content:
Long term listener from the early Party Room days. Still a fan of Fran, but can’t deal with the daily Politics Now deluge. It’s not that PK is on every day (although she is) it’s the constant self references, the talking about herself, her life, her opinions, her altruistic obsession of politics, the editorialising instead of reporting, the talking over guests with her own opinions. Just too much. Finding other podcasts now. 
If I could get just The Party Room as a podcast, I would probably still listen to that.

reviews.author: heysoulswifty
reviews.content: I love Politics Now and the Party Room - and because I do,  it goes without saying that I love PK too. As a daily and long term listener, I should rate and review more often, but I felt compelled to come and say how much I loved the Josh Burns interview. The combination of hearing the questions I would have like to asked my self and the self deprecating, honest and thoughtful answers, was a pleasure to listen to. The whole summer series was fab, but I loved this one the most. Thanks!

reviews.author: TegwanLC
reviews.content: For anyone with an ounce of media literacy, the way these podcasters frame Israel’s actions is difficult listening. Some very basic tips: try “systemic destruction” instead of “what’s happening” in Gaza. Try “mass murder” and “genocide” instead of “overreach”. Try applying some of the language you comfortably and fluently use to describe Hamas’s ideology and violence to the Israeli government which has wrought unspeakable horror in Gaza and the West Bank on a daily basis for years.

reviews.author: Krutas R
reviews.content: Long time listener, Fran and PK have such a great dynamic and the pacing of the podcast is always perfect - enough detail to keep you informed about the issues but with a focus on commentary and analysis so it doesn’t feel like you are listening to the news. Fran and PK’s passion and knowledge comes through each episode. Seeing a new episode released is always a highlight of Thursdays. Love your work! (Also don’t mind the daily feed with politics now as waiting a week is too long!)

title: ABC Cricket Podcast with Corbin Middlemas and Ed Cowan - ABC listen
description: Corbin Middlemas and ex-Test opener Ed Cowan deliver you the best analysis in cricket with a rolling conversation on Australia's national game. This cricket podcast gets you across the Test format, T20 and ODIs with thought provoking conversation.

episodes.title: Ryan Harris talks 'rhino rev ups', SACA glory and Australian coach aspirations
episodes.description: It's been a wildly successful two seasons for Ryan Harris in his first head coaching role with South Australia and he sits down with Corbin to talk us through his journey, philosophy and dreams.

episodes.title: George Bailey chats relationships with the press, retirements and Ashes reviews
episodes.description: Chief selector George Bailey is one of the most influential figures in Australian cricket and joins Corbin to talk through the life of a selector.

episodes.title: A "proper" Sheffield Shield final sees SACA triumph and the Vics buckle
episodes.description: "It was a classic", according to Corbin & Ed and it's hard to argue with that advertisement for long form Australian cricket with South Australia back to back Sheffield Shield champions for the first time in 124 seasons.

episodes.title: Straight up, this episode is MUST listen
episodes.description: If you’re craving some behind the scenes insights and thorough debate on BBL privatisation, the Brad Haddin appointment, a disgruntled Cam Green and a Shield final then you’ve come to the right place.

episodes.title: Shield final confirmed but the season batting numbers are grim reading
episodes.description: We know it will be Victoria vs South Australia in the Sheffield Shield final but the real question is, why have the runs been so hard to come by this season?

episodes.title: Reckoning with the depth of India's T20 dominance
episodes.description: India thumped NZ to make T20 World Cup history and Corbin and Ed can't see anyone competing with them in the near future.

episodes.title: T20 World Cups every two years just don't resonate
episodes.description: The T20 World Cup final awaits but the real question is - should this tournament continue to be staged every two years?!

episodes.title: T20 World Cup semis and Alyssa Healy's fairytale finale
episodes.description: Has there been a better finale in cricket than Alyssa Healy's day out in Hobart against India with a 150 and a cheeky couple of overs with the ball.

episodes.title: “I would hate it”: The possible BBL flow on of The Hundred’s Pakistan issue
episodes.description: As potential Pakistan player bans for Indian owned teams in The Hundred get debated in the UK, Corbin and Ed ponder the domino effect here in the BBL if the league is privatised.

episodes.title: Selectors under fire, South Africa shock India and the BBL money fight heats up
episodes.description: Australia are out of the T20 World Cup and the temperature has risen quickly. Corbin Middlemas and Ed Cowan unpack whether this was a planning failure, an injury crisis, or a warning sign for life beyond the “Big Three”.

reviews.author: Not a political journalist
reviews.content: I recently returned to listening to this podcast - around the  start of the 2025-26 Test series between Australia and England. The smugness/arrogance of Ed Cowan had previously bothered me a bit - but I was generally prepared to tolerate it, as I was appreciating Ed Cowan’s insights.  However, after listening to the November 2025 “live” episode recorded in a pub in inner Sydney, I don’t think I can take any more of Ed Cowan. In the pub setting, the smugness/arrogance became even more obvious - and the large amount of swearing was surprising. What was the purpose of the swearing? Was it alcohol-induced? If this was happening on most other media “platforms”, it would simply be annoying - but given that it was all taking place via the ABC (the national, public broadcaster), I think that some kind of formal disciplinary response to these issues may be warranted. I might start listening to The Guardian’s cricket podcast, instead.

reviews.author: Nate:))
reviews.content:
Hey guys, I have been listening for a while now and love all the podcasts. 

The Australian team is in a really weird spot with most our blokes on the back end of their time as bowlers and batters. As a suggestion, why keep all these blokes in for the final test when we have already one the series. Keep the essential players but anyone else, sub them in for younger blokes like Todd Murphy, Cooper Connolly, Nathan Mcsweeney etc. let them show the older blokes and the selectors what they have to offer

reviews.author: Shadow1940
reviews.content:
A podcast that flows really well, both have a balanced view of the cricketing landscape.

Love the behind the scenes insights that Ed gives; player t20 tournament salaries for example.

Corbin and Ed work in well together and it’s been really enjoyable and easy listening.

Be great if some of the other pods could be stand alone as well (as opposed to being lumped into the best of abc sport)… for example Corbin and Ben.

Thanks, Matt from Tassie

reviews.author: RemotelyMurph
reviews.content:
Alas guys you’ve lost me . 
You’re views on McSweeney’s selection ( averaging 97  in 24/25, Shield, 68 in Marsh Cup with runs for Australia A). the attempt at an explanation the following week and now a diatribe on SA cricket, not rating selections from SACA due to their lack of success is my tipping point for getting off.  Head wins Aust 2 trophies almost single-handedly  Carey rescues last test in NZ.  That is what success looks like!

reviews.author: Castlemaine Gus
reviews.content: Ed Cowan is thoughtful and erudite and really enjoying his take on current Australian series with India .... great to hear him nail racism as a problem for Australian society in general , sadly it is a very racist and punitive society and change is urgently needed . Corbyn does a great job as the consummate professional that he is . Thanks guys for a great podcast which has been  a saviour in lockdowns on the other side of the globe 😊

reviews.author: n/a double one triple two
reviews.content:
I enjoy the program, but not the idea of combining the full program and individual stories into one feed. You can make it work by setting up automatic downloads so that all segments released in the last 24 hours are downloaded, and then set it up so that it plays them from oldest to newest so that you get the top story first up. However, I don't see what was wrong with the old system! Plus, if you can't listen one morning for whatever reason, then rather than deleting the old automatically downloaded program and listening to the latest one, you have to delete each of the episodes individually.

Hopefully this won't cost the program too many listeners.

reviews.author: madeinoz
reviews.content:
I used to love the old format of all in one program, I moved kicking and screaming blue murder to the new individual format, however since moving to the new format of individual stories I actually quite like the new format.

Now for some reason I'm seeing the old format return to this feed however it's on the same channel as the short programs and honestly just clogs the feed.  

I automatically download all new unplayed episodes so the larger old format all in one program also gets downloaded so is wasting bandwidth as I end up deleting it as I've already listened to the other programs.  

Please please please seperate it out onto its own channel.

reviews.author: LTOGJO
reviews.content:
As a former teacher and school counsellor (psychologist) in the NSW education system, I was very interested to hear the discussion on the topic of school refusal. This is nothing new. It all comes back to the same old issue of the under resourcing of public education and over working teachers and counsellors. 

As a counsellor, I was spread over three schools while working part-time for 3 days per week. I had a case load of around 30 students per school and I could never get through the work. 

When I first began counselling in 2003, there were funding cuts. So, children with language learning difficulties no longer received in-school support from a teacher’s aide. Also, children with “low average” IQ scores (80 - 89) were in mainstream classes with no additional support. 

The localities in which I worked were very high needs and there were children from refugee families, children with English as a second language and children whose parents were not literate in their own language. Teachers were overwhelmed, stressed and sometimes depressed.

There was never enough time to complete everything expected and classroom teachers were not trained well enough to support children with specific learning needs such as autism, apraxia, dyspraxia or specific mental health issues. In NSW, so called medical issues such as epilepsy were not funded. I remember one case where a child was enduring numerous petite mal episodes every day and her mother could not understand why she was not receiving support. She was justifiably angry,

The recent upsurge in school refusal is a symptom of a much deeper and prolonged problem. The fact that it is happening now, after the pandemic, may be because some children have realised that they can learn at home via technology and thus not have to endure being singled out as “different” and to cope with the bullying that often follows.

My suggestion to the mother of the children cited in your segment today, is to approach her MP and to enlist the support of her Parents and Citizens local and state group to begin lobbying governments for better funding and more appropriate training for teachers and all school staff. The Australian Education Union of Victoria may also be able to help. Also, as she would be aware, there are organisations that support children with autism and their parents. They may also be willing to lobby. It is only when governments feel they have a mandate and when issues become noisy and political that change occurs.

reviews.author: Mischa of Oz
reviews.content:
I use to enjoy this show and find its analysis of current news and politics refreshing and insightful, but I’ve found that it is increasingly under-selling itself by giving too much attention to cheap topics that pander to audiences’ easy-to-access fear and frustration: insurance, banking, cost-of-living, Trump, etc. There is nothing inherently wrong with these topics, but the show tends to address them in a slightly tedious way akin to something I’d expect from au audio version of Today Tonight. The presenter also puts an unusual amount of personal experience and feeling into their delivery and interviews. Again, there is nothing inherently wrong with this, but it’s not appropriate for an objective news and analysis program (and more appropriate for a podcast or opinion piece).

Maybe I should be listening to something like the 7am podcast instead, but I thought something closer to that would be more appropriate for the usual ABC audience in its News Daily show. The ABC’s ‘This Week’ was a good example of the tone and sophistication of analysis that I would like to see in a daily show.

title: ABC SPORT DAILY with Patrick Stack - ABC listen
description: ABC SPORT Daily is your guide to the top sports news stories of the day. We dive behind the headlines of the day to get you up to speed with everything that's making news.

episodes.title: The emotional toll of Alexa Leary's traumatic brain injury
episodes.description: You might have seen Paralympian Alexa Leary winning gold medals, dancing on the pool deck and giving the most bubbly and joyous interviews.

episodes.title: Does the Lance Collard hearing raise more questions than answers?
episodes.description: St Kilda’s Lance Collard has been handed a nine-week suspension from the AFL tribunal for a homophobic slur during a VFL match last month.

episodes.title: Patrick Johnson on the Australian sprinters coming for his record
episodes.description: Gout Gout and Lachie Kennedy were the headline acts at the 2026 Australian Athletics Championships and they didn’t disappoint.

episodes.title: Is Rory McIlroy's second Masters the start of his second act?
episodes.description: Because there's only one thing better than one green jacket. Rory McIlroy has made history again by winning consecutive Masters on a rollercoaster Sunday at Augusta and it might signal a second surge from one of golf's greats.

episodes.title: Fri Fix: The NRL heads west, will AFL's Wildcard Round do the same?
episodes.description: With the Perth Bears joining the competition next year, the double header in Perth this weekend feels extra important for the NRL.

episodes.title: Are we gathering 'round in Adelaide for the last time?
episodes.description: All 18 teams in the AFL are headed to Adelaide for Gather Round this weekend but with the deal between the league and South Australia expiring after this year, the future of the concept is up in the air.

episodes.title: The Rory v Bryson rivalry reignites as McIlroy looks to defend his Masters crown
episodes.description: When Rory McIlroy won the 2025 Masters you sensed that a weight lifted off his shoulders, this year he's returning to Augusta looking to go back-to-back.

episodes.title: Stawell Gift win just the beginning for Femi Komolafe
episodes.description: Femi Komolafe is 21 years old, a medical student and is now the winner of the Stawell Gift.

episodes.title: Raw, freezing, stunning: how Ireland became a big wave mecca
episodes.description: If you think about the biggest waves in the world… what comes to mind? Pipeline, Hawaii? Nazare, Portugal… the lighthouse watching over monsters rolling in? Mavericks, California? Teahupoo, Tahiti?

episodes.title: ‘Just admit it’: Molly Picklum’s not so secret list
episodes.description: Molly Picklum enters the 2026 season in unfamiliar territory; she's the hunted not the hunter. Some might find that dynamic uncomfortable. However, Picklum has a not-so-secret weapon; her 'just admit it' list.

reviews.author: Rebecca_K_M
reviews.content: This show consistently interviews experts in their relevant sport, so you’re always hearing a diverse range of voices and opinions. It provides an in depth episode about topical sports news and then sprinkle in some bite sized sporting updates all in a neat little package under 15mins in length. It’s a great way to consume sporting news on a daily basis.

reviews.author: Aussie Woz
reviews.content: A short, sharp listen that covers so much sporting ground. I thought I knew many sports well but the team have dug deep into ones that I wasn’t even aware of.  This is done with interesting experts, some well known and some not, but it really works. Thanks for doing this you are clearly an awesome team!

reviews.author: AE listener
reviews.content:
Love the variety of sports. Podcasts has interesting content and great production. 

Twice I have listened to this podcasts covers the same topic as the abc news podcast, and I find this one more interesting and engaging. 

However I do agree with other comments saying there could be less rugby.

reviews.author: Chatham Chamber
reviews.content: I regard this podcast as essential listening for sports fans.  The form of the podcast - <15 minutes on a single topic - means you get considered, thorough analysis of a topic. The questions are insightful and lead to revealing answers.  Patrick Stack has raised the bar for sports journalism.

reviews.author: 
reviews.content: This is a great podcast. Short sharp and very succinct. Covers all sports. Unlike other podcasts that focus almost exclusively on AFL which is only played in one country (and only in some states). This podcast covers all sports, popular much more important sports. Fantastic podcast.

title: ABC TassieCast with Airlie Ward - ABC listen
description: Each Friday, Airlie Ward chats with Tasmania's top journos to unpack one of the big stories of the week. If it's going to hit your heart, head or your hip pocket – we're going to break it down for you.

episodes.title: Will land sales future-proof Tassie's only uni?
episodes.description: Tasmania has a long tradition of young people growing up, spreading their wings, and leaving for the mainland - before for some, returning to the island.

episodes.title: Do we care enough about our pollies' mental health?
episodes.description: In what's believed to be the biggest study of its kind, a staggering 70 percent of almost 300 of our federal, state and local politicians who took part say the job has adversely affected their mental health.

episodes.title: Easter plans under the pump as Tassies shell out for fuel and choccy
episodes.description: Many of us are already feeling the pinch ... We've got massive fuel prices, TT Line has added a surcharge, farmers are worried about future production capacity add to that the Easter Bunny is more expensive than ever.

episodes.title: The manosphere creeping into Tassie classrooms
episodes.description: The manosphere - the online world considered responsible for the rise in anti-social behaviour and fuelling misogyny is reaching Tassie classrooms. So how and why are men, particular young men getting caught up in this manosphere web?

episodes.title: Kunanyi/Mt Wellington: A mountain of a debate
episodes.description: Kunanyi/Mt Wellington is Tasmania's most visited natural asset but is a cable car the answer to getting more people on the mountain?

episodes.title: Tassie's greyhound industry ... is the gate about to close?
episodes.description: In 2025 there were more than 200 injuries to greyhounds recorded on the track. Many countries have phased the industry out amid animal cruelty concerns ... could Tassie be the first Australian state to do it?

episodes.title: Inside a Hobart community needle exchange program
episodes.description: When you imagine someone using a needle exchange program, who do you picture? Chances are, it’s not always who you’d expect.

episodes.title: Is that a side of antibiotics with your seafood?
episodes.description: After its public image took a dive last summer when millions of fish died ... the salmon industry sought regulatory approval to use an antibiotic in a bid to prevent more mass deaths.

episodes.title: Has the state government squibbed on gambling reform?
episodes.description: Imagine what you could do with 200 million dollars. That's how much money Tasmanians lost on pokies last financial year,

episodes.title: Is it time Tassie declared wild deer a pest?
episodes.description: They might look like Bambi but they're making a big mess. There are tens of thousands of fallow deer trampling across the landscape and they now outnumber some of our most iconic species. Featuring reporter Meg Whitfield.
